summary:
LunaSight is an interactive web tool that helps mission planners, educators, and the public quickly compare candidate landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. The user selects a site and a date range, and the tool shows where the Sun and Earth are relative to the local horizon, taking the surrounding terrain into account.

For each site, LunaSight calculates sunlight availability, which shows the potential for solar power, and direct-to-Earth visibility, which shows communication windows. It displays the results as a horizon view, a timeline, and simple scores. Users can place several sites side by side and immediately see which one offers the most sunlight and the longest contact with Earth.

Existing tools give accurate data, but their interfaces are complex and slow to use. LunaSight turns the same information into a clear visual comparison, which makes early mission planning faster. It also makes lunar exploration easier for students and the public to understand.
details:
**What it does.** Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a desktop application that shows, for any place at the Moon's south pole and any date from 2025 to 2035, whether a lander there has sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication, and for how long. At the pole the Sun never climbs more than about 1.5° above the horizon and the Earth stays within a few degrees of it, so the surrounding mountains and crater rims decide everything. Our tool puts the Sun and the Earth against the real terrain horizon and turns the result into a picture anyone can read.

**How you use it.** Pick a site from the list or double-click any point on the polar map, then drag the time cursor or press Play. Five linked views update together:

- a list of candidate sites with the share of time each one has sunlight, an Earth link, and both, for side-by-side comparison;

- a 3D terrain model, 40 × 40 km around the site, with sunlight and cast shadows computed from real elevation data;

- a live sunlight map of the whole polar region for the selected moment;

- a 360° horizon panorama showing the skyline the lander would see, with the Sun and Earth at their true positions;

- a timeline of sunlight and Earth-link windows over 7 days to a full year.

A status panel gives the numbers a planner needs: azimuth, elevation, clearance above the terrain, time to the next sunset or loss of link, the longest darkness and the longest communication gap.

**How it works.** Sun and Earth positions come from the NASA JPL Horizons System. We download one compact hourly table of the sub-solar and sub-Earth points and compute azimuth and elevation for any lunar site from it; the result matches Horizons' own per-site output to about 0.005°. Terrain is the LRO LOLA south-polar elevation model at 80 m per pixel. For each site we cast rays in 720 directions out to 250 km over the curved Moon to get its horizon profile. The Sun or the Earth counts as visible when more than half of its disk is above the terrain in its direction. The horizon algorithm is implemented twice, in Python for pre-computation and in C++ for points the user picks, and the two agree within 0.02°.

**What it shows.** For the year 2027 the tool makes the central trade-off visible. Shackleton's Connecting Ridge is sunlit 88% of the time but sees the Earth only 51% of the time, with gaps of about two weeks. Mons Mouton, a few degrees toward the near side, sees the Earth 76% of the time but is sunlit only 40%. A mission has to choose between light and link, and the tool lets a planner see that choice for any site and date in seconds.

**Benefits and intended impact.** Mission planners can compare sites and dates without scripting ephemeris tools. Educators can show why the lunar south pole is both attractive and difficult. The public can explore real NASA data through a picture instead of a table.

**Tools and technologies.** C++17, Qt 6.5 (Qt Quick, Qt Quick 3D), Python with NumPy for data preparation, CMake, FFmpeg for the demo video. Data: NASA JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA polar gridded elevation model (PDS), NASA Blue Marble.

**What is creative about it.** Lighting is not painted on: the shadows in the 3D view and on the map are ray-traced on the CPU from the elevation model for the exact date and hour, so the picture is a physical result. Any point on the map can become a landing site with one double-click.

**What we considered, and limits.** NASA publishes candidate regions about 15 km across, not exact landing points, so our site coordinates are representative points inside those regions. The elevation model has 80 m resolution, so boulders and small craters are not modelled, and slope and landing safety are not assessed. The percentages come from the precise horizon profile; the 3D view and the map use a faster, slightly coarser shadow calculation.

**Use of AI.** This project was developed with an AI coding assistant (Claude). The team defined the concept and the architecture, chose Qt Quick 3D as the platform and NASA JPL Horizons and LRO LOLA as the data sources, directed the work and reviewed the results. The AI assistant was used to write application code and data-preparation scripts under that direction, to draft this description and the slides, to script and render the demo video, and to synthesise its soundtrack. All Sun, Earth and terrain data are real NASA data and were not generated by AI.
